item.title: PLACES
item.description: The rooms, corners, and addresses of New York where the MAP’s history happened.

item.title: Bernard Herrmann
item.description: Alfred Hitchcock wanted the shower scene in Psycho to play in silence.

item.title: Brian Eno
item.description: On Roxy Music’s first two records there is an instrument the credits can’t quite name: the rest of the band, fed through Brian Eno’s synthesizer and sent back out transformed.

item.title: Curtis Mayfield
item.description: The sound that made Curtis Mayfield unmistakable was built from a child’s shortcut.

item.title: George Harrison
item.description: George Harrison played as if notes cost money. Few guitarists in rock played with less waste.

item.title: Ryuichi Sakamoto
item.description: As a Tokyo high schooler, Ryuichi Sakamoto rode a packed commuter train twenty minutes every morning and started counting the noise.

item.title: Burt Bacharach
item.description: Burt Bacharach is the most harmonically sophisticated songwriter in the history of American pop — the figure who brought Ravel, Debussy, and Brazilian bossa nova into the three-minute single without sacrificing emotional accessibility.

item.title: The Beatles
item.description: One chord opens A Hard Day’s Night, and no two musicians have ever agreed how to name it.

item.title: British Invasion

item.title: Swinging Sixties
item.description: For a few years in the middle of the 1960s, the rest of the world looked to a handful of streets in the West End of London to see what the young would do next.
